parakeet: Now, this also reveals a deeper problem within apologetic Christianity. And since you stayed around for all three assumptions, this part is just for you. Apologetics train Christians to ask irrelevant questions of unqualified sources. Apologetic Christianity often doesn't teach people to become more curious, informed, or intellectually responsible. It teaches them to become rhetorically confident in areas where they're not actually qualified. So the Christian is not asking what do cosmologists currently understand about the origin and expansion of the universe. They're asking how can I use the fact that most people don't understand cosmology to make my belief seem more reasonable? And that's where a societal danger comes in. Once people are trained to use public ignorance as a stage for confidence, they can do that with anything. It creates a habit of bypassing expertise while performing certainty in front of people who also do not know enough to challenge the performance. The problem with apologetics is not simply that it gives Christians bad answers, it often trains Christians to ask bad questions in the wrong rooms for the wrong reasons. If you genuinely want to understand the origins of the universe, there are cosmologists, physicists, philosophers of science, academic journals, lectures, conferences, textbooks, and entire fields of study dedicated to that question. But apologetics usually doesn't send Christians there, it sends them to the comment section, the dinner table, the college campus sidewalk, the debate stage, or the atheist friend who never claimed to be a cosmologist. Apologetics often majors in areas of common ignorance among common people instead of directing people toward the disciplines where those questions are actually being studied seriously. It doesn't solve the ignorance problem, it exploits the ignorance gap. The ignorance gap is the space between what ordinary people do not know and what experts have spent their lives studying. Apologetics often live inside that gap, not because it wants to close it, but because that gap is rhetorically useful.
